paragraphs.heading: Bounds on a union
paragraphs.text: Boole's inequality, stated for a finite number of events, can be stretched into a family of upper and lower bounds. These bounds limit the probability of a finite union of events from above and from below. They carry the name of Carlo Emilio Bonferroni, and his work is cited as Bonferroni (1936).

paragraphs.heading: Where they come from
paragraphs.text: The Bonferroni inequalities are consequences of the inclusion–exclusion principle. Boole's inequality sits inside the family as the special case where K = 1. Boole's inequality itself comes in a finite version and a countable version. The countable one is reached from the finite one by letting the number of events n grow without end and using the continuity from below of probability measures.

paragraphs.heading: Not only for probability
paragraphs.text: Proving the inclusion–exclusion principle needs very little: only that P is finitely additive and never negative. Because of that, the Bonferroni inequalities keep working when P is swapped for any finite content, a notion from measure theory. In the same spirit, Boole's inequality is a case of the countable subadditivity of measures, so it holds for arbitrary measures and not just probability measures.

paragraphs.heading: A five-part estimate
paragraphs.text: Picture a task where you estimate five parameters from one random sample, and you can tune the accuracy of each one on its own. You want all five estimates to be good at once, with a 95% chance. The question is how strict to be with each single estimate. One answer is to set each of them to 0.05/5 = 0.01, which is 1%.

paragraphs.heading: The Bonferroni method
paragraphs.text: Put another way, each single estimate must be made good to 99%, for instance by building a 99% confidence interval for it. Doing that for all five guarantees that the whole set of estimates is good with a 95% chance. This recipe is known as the Bonferroni Method of simultaneous inference.
